description: Building Mars Pathfinder for the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge - a layered, integrated view of Jezero Crater that pulls together data from multiple NASA science missions to help a human explorer plan and carry out a successful Marswalk.
summary: Mars Pathfinder is an offline route planner and survival monitor for walking on Mars. It uses real NASA HiRISE terrain data from the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (an elevation model plus imagery) to find the safest efficient path between two points. The A* search, verified against Dijkstra’s algorithm, treats steep slopes, rough ground and no-data areas as hazards: it will not cross them, and it penalises rough terrain. For each route it reports distance, elevation change, travel time and an estimated oxygen use and CO₂ production, so an astronaut can see what a trip would cost before leaving, even with no contact with base. Mission Control combines a 2D terrain map with a 3D Mars globe (including thermal and elevation layers and several exploration targets), graded alerts for life-support and medical supplies, and a data page listing every source and limitation. It matters because EVA planning is a safety problem: people need to know the effort and risk of each step. This is a research prototype with hypothetical life-support inputs, not a flight system.
details:
What it does. Mars Pathfinder plans walking routes across real Martian terrain and estimates what each trip costs. It uses a NASA HiRISE digital elevation model and orthoimage of an area near Jezero Crater, resampled to an 8 m grid. Slope and a roughness measure are computed from the elevation model. An A* search, checked against Dijkstra’s algorithm (same optimal cost, about 27% fewer cells searched), finds the cheapest safe path. Steep slopes, rough ground and no-data cells are excluded, and rough ground is penalised. For each route the app shows distance, elevation change, travel time and an estimated oxygen use and CO₂ production. Mission Control also has graded alerts for life-support and medical supplies, a 2D map with layers and contours, and a 3D Mars globe with thermal and elevation layers and several exploration targets.

Benefits and impact. An astronaut can see the effort and risk of an excursion before leaving, even without contact with base. The whole app is one offline file with the terrain embedded. A data page lists every source and limitation.

Tools. Python, NumPy, Pillow and OpenCV for data processing and the tested routing engine; HTML, CSS and JavaScript (canvas and WebGL) for the app; Three.js for the globe.

Creative. Obstacle-aware planning on real data in a single file, with proposed and hypothetical values labelled throughout.

Factors considered. Honesty about data (the medical and life-support figures are demo values and the alert thresholds are unverified), safety defaults, accessibility, and offline use. It is a research prototype, not a flight system.
